hyperedges.label: Deliberate defects that must stay broken
Adding a concurrency slice end to end
Making a race deterministic without flaky tests
Process-local state that silently stops working at N replicas
The machinery that makes a race reproduce 100% of the time
Blocked CDN, no Docker daemon, no proxy egress — constraints that decided three ADRs
The coordination point must live in shared state, not process memory
Two correct strategies paying in different currencies
The family of concurrency failure modes

nodes.label: ADR-0001 Vertical slice architecture
nodes.rationale: Layering would split a withdrawal's read-modify-write across four projects, hiding the race the repo exists to show; IAccountRepository.Update looks identical for a blind overwrite and a version-checked update. Modular monolith solves a team-boundary problem this single-context repo does not have. Accepted costs: no compile-time dependency enforcement, deliberate duplication between slices, and unfamiliarity to reviewers who expect Clean architecture.

nodes.label: ADR-0002 Plain handler classes, no MediatR
nodes.rationale: MediatR is commercially licensed and a public teaching repo should not carry a paid dependency; more importantly its pipeline hides the exact lines that race. A hand-rolled dispatcher would reproduce the indirection without the ecosystem — worst of both. Costs accepted: no pipeline behaviours, endpoints depend on concrete handler types, scales badly past a few dozen handlers.
nodes.norm_label: adr-0002 plain handler classes, no mediatr

nodes.label: NaiveWithdrawHandler (deliberately lossy)
nodes.rationale: Performs an unguarded read-decide-write and is supposed to lose updates; tests assert that it does. Fixing it removes the lesson.

nodes.label: InMemoryAccountStore (unsafe singleton on purpose)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately not thread-safe at the account level and registered as a singleton. Adding a lock or scoping it per-request silently deletes the bug the repo is built to demonstrate.

nodes.label: ScaleEndpoints sync-over-async endpoint
nodes.rationale: Calls .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on purpose to demonstrate thread-pool starvation under load.

nodes.label: InterestStrategies ParallelWithLock / ParallelWithConcurrentQueue
nodes.rationale: Slow on purpose — the 'I parallelised it and it got slower' result.

nodes.label: Warnings are errors (CS9113)
nodes.rationale: TreatWarningsAsErrors in Directory.Build.props turns an unread primary-constructor parameter into a build failure; use the parameter or drop it.

nodes.label: No commercially-licensed dependencies
nodes.rationale: MediatR, FluentAssertions and NBomber rejected on licence grounds so a reader can use the same approach at work; Shouldly and an in-repo load harness replace them.

nodes.label: Gate before acquiring a lock
nodes.rationale: Gating inside a critical section deadlocks: the lock holder waits at a barrier for actors who cannot enter until it releases.

nodes.label: Only the first retry attempt joins the barrier
nodes.rationale: Retrying actors that re-join a barrier stall the run until the 5s timeout, because actors that already finished never arrive.
nodes.norm_label: only the first retry attempt joins the barrier

nodes.label: Fresh DbContext per retry attempt
nodes.rationale: Reusing one keeps the stale entity in the change tracker, so the retry re-sends the same doomed UPDATE forever.

nodes.label: xmin is a PostgreSQL system column
nodes.rationale: Not included in SELECT *, so raw SQL must say SELECT *, xmin FROM "Accounts" or EF fails to materialise the entity.
nodes.norm_label: xmin is a postgresql system column

nodes.label: DbContext is not thread-safe
nodes.rationale: Concurrent actors each need their own context from IDbContextFactory<BankDbContext>.

nodes.label: Money is decimal, cents are long
nodes.norm_label: money is decimal, cents are long

nodes.label: No Docker daemon in this environment
nodes.rationale: The 3-replica demo has only ever been `docker compose config`-validated; claiming it was run would be false.
nodes.norm_label: no docker daemon in this environment

nodes.label: IWithdrawStrategy
nodes.rationale: Must be registered as a singleton in Program.cs — an unregistered strategy compiles and silently never appears in /api/lab/strategies.

nodes.label: IContentionRecorder
nodes.rationale: Called from inside the code under observation, so it must never block, do I/O or throw; use Interlocked for counters and push SignalR fan-out to the background ContentionBroadcaster.

nodes.label: IAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Two implementations behind one interface; swapping the DI registration is the entire scale-out lesson.

nodes.label: InProcessAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Correct on one instance only — process memory is not shared between replicas.

nodes.label: PostgresAdvisoryAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Survives any number of instances because the coordination point is the database.

nodes.label: Gate placement rule
nodes.rationale: Lock-taking handlers gate at BeforeAcquire, lock-free handlers at AfterRead; the 5-second gate cap is a safety net, not a licence to gate in the wrong place.

nodes.label: RunSummaryCalculator
nodes.rationale: Every verdict — who won, who lost silently, whether money was conserved — is computed server-side here and tested; the UI must not recompute or second-guess it.

nodes.label: Signals, no NgRx
nodes.rationale: The UI is a presentation surface; a state library would add ceremony that teaches nothing about concurrency.

nodes.label: CORS must allow localhost and 127.0.0.1
nodes.rationale: A browser treats them as different origins, so allowing one makes every call fail as if the API were down; a wildcard origin is impossible because SignalR needs AllowCredentials.

nodes.label: SignalR groups are per-process
nodes.rationale: Behind more than one replica this needs a Redis backplane; without one clients silently miss events, so the live feed is an accelerator and the REST timeline stays the source of truth.

nodes.label: Never assert an ordering you did not force
nodes.rationale: Asserting a specific actor won is asserting the scheduler's mood and will fail eventually; assert only what holds under every interleaving.
nodes.norm_label: never assert an ordering you did not force

nodes.label: Relative-only timing assertions
nodes.rationale: Absolute upper bounds flake on a loaded machine; absolute lower bounds derived from the work are fine. Two performance-ratio assertions were deleted in M5 after failing under CPU load — ratios belong in BenchmarkDotNet, which has warmup and error bars.

nodes.label: TimingSensitiveCollection
nodes.rationale: Disables parallelisation so an elapsed-time test is not competing with three others for the same cores.

nodes.label: Three-tier test strategy
nodes.rationale: Deterministic tests may assert a specific forced interleaving; invariant tests assert only what holds under every interleaving; integration tests against real PostgreSQL are the only place concurrency tokens and row locks are real.

nodes.label: InvariantSuiteHasTeethTests
nodes.rationale: Points the invariants at the naive handler and requires them to fail; if they start passing the suite has stopped applying pressure.

nodes.label: No EF Core in-memory provider for integration tests
nodes.rationale: It implements neither concurrency tokens nor row locks, so tests would pass against a system that is still broken.
nodes.norm_label: no ef core in-memory provider for integration tests

nodes.label: ADR template with mandatory sections
nodes.rationale: Why not the others, Trade-offs accepted and Interview angle are mandatory and hook-checked: a decision you cannot argue against is a default you inherited, and an ADR with no downside listed is a rationalisation.

nodes.label: Every measured claim must be real
nodes.rationale: A benchmark whose conditions you cannot state is a number, not evidence; figures came from a 4-core shared VM under a ShortRun job with wide error bars.
nodes.norm_label: every measured claim must be real

nodes.label: IInterleaveGate seam
nodes.rationale: A testability hook deliberately placed on the production hot path: NoOpInterleaveGate in production, ScriptedInterleaveGate in tests, making the lost update 100% reproducible instead of a race test that hopes for a collision.

nodes.label: Concurrency vs parallelism mental model
nodes.rationale: One teller juggling many customers (interleaved, async over I/O) versus many tellers at many counters (simultaneous, needs cores).

nodes.label: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency
nodes.rationale: Contention rate is the deciding variable: rare collisions favour detect-and-retry, common collisions on hot rows favour queue-and-wait; long user think time forbids holding a DB lock.

nodes.label: Scaling as three layers
nodes.rationale: Application code (how it waits), instances (Kubernetes multiplies instances but cannot fix code sharing mutable process memory), then data (row contention, not CPU, is the wall).

nodes.label: Silent losers in RunSummary
nodes.rationale: Actors whose write was overwritten and who were told they succeeded — the punchline of the whole lab.

nodes.label: .NET 8 LTS forced by blocked CDN
nodes.rationale: builds.dotnet.microsoft.com is proxy-blocked (403), so dotnet-install.sh fails and .NET 9/10 cannot be obtained in this environment.

nodes.label: Thread-pool starvation result (979 vs 35 RPS)
nodes.rationale: One .Result instead of await collapses throughput from 979 to 35 RPS and p99 from 105 ms to 3531 ms on identical hardware.

nodes.label: In-process lock breaks across three replicas
nodes.rationale: No application code changes between the two compose files; only process memory stops being shared, which is enough to break every strategy whose coordination lives in process memory while optimistic, pessimistic and advisory-lock strategies keep working.
nodes.norm_label: in-process lock breaks across three replicas

nodes.label: net8.0 as pinned target framework
nodes.rationale: Chosen because builds.dotnet.microsoft.com is blocked by the proxy (HTTP 403), so dotnet-install.sh cannot fetch .NET 9/10; Ubuntu's archive carries dotnet-sdk-8.0. .NET 8 is also the most widely deployed enterprise LTS, matching interview reality. Accepted cost: .NET 8 leaves support before .NET 10, and roll-forward can confuse readers on newer SDKs.

nodes.label: System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9+)
nodes.rationale: A dedicated lock type replacing lock-on-object, avoiding the classic mistake of locking on something publicly reachable like `this` or a string. Cannot be demonstrated in running code here; covered as text in lesson 02 instead.

nodes.label: Multi-targeting net8.0;net10.0 (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Rejected: doubles build and test time and forces #if NET10_0_OR_GREATER branches through teaching code to demonstrate one keyword. Better described in a lesson than built into the project structure.

nodes.label: Directory.Build.props central pinning
nodes.rationale: TargetFramework pinned once for all five projects so the eventual upgrade is a one-line change plus a package bump.

nodes.label: CS1705 assembly-version build break
nodes.rationale: Package versions must stay on a mutually consistent 8.0.x line (EF Core 8.0.11, Npgsql 8.0.11); mixing 8.0.11 and 8.0.13 produced CS1705 once during setup.

nodes.label: ADR-0004 Hybrid persistence: in-memory and PostgreSQL
nodes.norm_label: adr-0004 hybrid persistence: in-memory and postgresql

nodes.label: Hybrid storage split (group A in-memory, group B PostgreSQL)
nodes.rationale: Postgres everywhere would smother the first lesson behind four EF concepts (change tracker, unit of work, when SaveChanges emits SQL, changed-column UPDATE) and make the naive race harder to reproduce. In-memory everywhere would make the optimistic/pessimistic slices lies — DbUpdateConcurrencyException never raised, SELECT FOR UPDATE a comment. Accepted cost: two persistence models to hold in your head and non-zero setup.
nodes.norm_label: hybrid storage split (group a in-memory, group b postgresql)

nodes.label: InMemoryAccountStore (singleton, deliberately unsafe)
nodes.rationale: Registered as a singleton because shared mutable process state is the precondition for the race; scoping it would quietly delete the bug. Duplicates the database's Version and a TryWrite compare-and-swap on purpose, to show optimistic concurrency is a pattern rather than an EF feature. Process-local, so it misbehaves under multiple replicas — which is the point of ADR-0014.

nodes.label: EF Core in-memory provider (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Not a shortcut: it implements neither concurrency tokens nor row locking, so tests would pass against a system that is still broken.

nodes.label: static ConcurrentDictionary as source of truth (trap)
nodes.rationale: Works perfectly on one instance and corrupts silently on two — the failure mode this repo demonstrates on purpose. Legitimate in-memory state is caches you can afford to lose, per-request scoped state, and single-writer designs.
nodes.norm_label: static concurrentdictionary as source of truth (trap)

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 16
nodes.rationale: Free, no licence acceptance, small footprint, real row-level locking, xmin as a schema-free concurrency token, and advisory locks for distributed locking with no extra infrastructure. Decisive here: no Docker daemon, while PostgreSQL 16 was already installed and startable natively.

nodes.label: xmin system column as concurrency token
nodes.rationale: Mapped as Version with type xid; costs nothing in schema because pg_attribute.attnum = -2 makes Npgsql's migration generator emit no DDL. Postgres-specific: porting to SQL Server means a byte[] RowVersion with [Timestamp].
nodes.norm_label: xmin system column as concurrency token

nodes.label: SELECT … FOR UPDATE row locking
nodes.rationale: Standard SQL, and it ports to SQL Server as WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK).

nodes.label: SQLite (rejected on capability)
nodes.rationale: Locking is file/database-level, not row-level — writers serialise across the whole database, so a pessimistic lock on one account is indistinguishable from a lock on every account. No SELECT FOR UPDATE, no meaningful deadlock scenario; a test proving pessimistic locking works would pass for the wrong reason.

nodes.label: SQL Server (rejected on friction)
nodes.rationale: The close call, lost on friction rather than merit: large image, EULA acceptance, more memory than a lab container has, and no Docker daemon in this environment. Its rowversion token is the more familiar one to .NET developers, which ADR-0006 covers explicitly.

nodes.label: ADR-0007 Optimistic by default, pessimistic by exception
nodes.norm_label: adr-0007 optimistic by default, pessimistic by exception

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency as the default
nodes.rationale: Measured on identical input (5 actors, 100 each, 100 balance, forced race): optimistic 9 attempts / 4 conflicts / 0.0 ms waiting vs pessimistic 5 attempts / 0 conflicts / 244.1 ms waiting. Optimistic holds no locks across requests so it scales horizontally. Accepted costs: retry logic in every write path, a failure mode that only appears under load, and starvation because retries have no queue.

nodes.label: Pessimistic used deliberately for named reasons
nodes.rationale: Reserved for hot rows, work expensive to redo, and first-come-first-served business rules. Pessimistic-by-default was rejected because it couples correctness to holding a resource: every waiter occupies a connection, deadlock becomes a standing risk on multi-entity operations, and it is incompatible with user think time.
nodes.norm_label: pessimistic used deliberately for named reasons

nodes.label: OptimisticWithdrawHandler.MaxAttempts = 5
nodes.rationale: Bounded retry: exhausting attempts returns a refusal rather than looping, because unbounded retry under contention is a livelock — everything busy, nothing progressing — and harder to diagnose than a deadlock since nothing looks stuck.

nodes.label: Only the first attempt joins the interleaving barrier
nodes.rationale: Retries must not re-join, because by then some actors have finished and would never arrive, so the barrier would stall the rest until its timeout.
nodes.norm_label: only the first attempt joins the interleaving barrier

nodes.label: Conflict rate as the deciding variable
nodes.rationale: Rough thresholds: under ~1% of writes conflicting, optimistic is comfortable; over ~10% you do more work retrying than a lock would cost. The better answer is to ask whether the hot row can be removed — shard the counter, queue the writes, event-source it.
nodes.norm_label: conflict rate as the deciding variable

nodes.label: Jittered exponential backoff (named, not implemented)
nodes.rationale: Production advice this repo names but does not implement: retrying immediately means the same actors collide again in the same order.

nodes.label: ADR-0008 A test-controlled interleaving seam in production code
nodes.norm_label: adr-0008 a test-controlled interleaving seam in production code

nodes.label: IInterleaveGate injected seam
nodes.rationale: The most arguable decision in the repo. Handlers call gate.ReachAsync at one named checkpoint; a no-op in production, a barrier when a run opts into a forced race. Defensible because forceRace is a product feature (a real runtime caller, not test-only) and because without it the project's central claim — deterministic, reproducible races — is false. In a real banking service it should be compiled out behind #if DEBUG, a build-stripped feature flag, or InternalsVisibleTo.

nodes.label: LabInterleaveGate
nodes.rationale: Returns Task.CompletedTask after a single ConcurrentDictionary lookup unless a run registered itself as a forced race; the gate caps forcing at 5 seconds so a mis-placed checkpoint cannot hang forever.

nodes.label: InterleaveCheckpoints (AfterRead / BeforeAcquire)
nodes.rationale: AfterRead for lock-free strategies, BeforeAcquire for locking ones. Proven during development: the locking handler originally gated inside its critical section, so the lock holder waited at a barrier for actors who could not enter until it released — a real deadlock. Checkpoint choice is part of writing a slice, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: AsyncBarrier
nodes.rationale: Exists because System.Threading.Barrier blocks its thread — using it would mean N thread-pool threads blocked waiting on each other, the very starvation bug lesson 09 is about. The lab would cause the problem it teaches.

nodes.label: Thread.Sleep/Task.Delay in the handler (rejected)
nodes.rationale: The worst option and the most commonly reached for: makes the race likelier but never certain, slows every run including production, and the delay is a magic number simultaneously too short on loaded CI and too long everywhere else.

nodes.label: Statistical brute force (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Slow and still non-deterministic; it inverts the assertion so a test cannot distinguish a lost update from an unrelated fault, and it cannot express specific interleavings such as 'all five actors read before any writes'.

nodes.label: Microsoft Coyote / CHESS deterministic schedulers
nodes.rationale: Systematically explore interleavings rather than sampling them; naming Coyote signals awareness that a hand-rolled barrier is the small version of a solved problem class.

nodes.label: ADR-0009 SignalR for the live timeline
nodes.norm_label: adr-0009 signalr for the live timeline

nodes.label: SignalR live contention feed
nodes.rationale: Chosen over SSE because SignalR's group model gives per-run fan-out for free and because SignalR is itself a standard .NET interview topic. Polling the finished run is kept as a fallback and for replay, but loses the property that matters: seeing events arrive while contention is happening.

nodes.label: ContentionHub (WatchRun / StopWatchingRun)
nodes.rationale: Clients join group run-{id}. Groups live in the process, so with multiple replicas a client on instance 2 misses events published on instance 1 — the same bug as the in-process lock, in a different costume.

nodes.label: ContentionBroadcaster BackgroundService
nodes.rationale: Drains the recorder's channel so a slow or broken client can never slow down a bank withdrawal; broadcast failures are logged and swallowed. Pushing inline from Record() would put a network call inside the critical section being measured.

nodes.label: Server-Sent Events (rejected, close call)
nodes.rationale: Arguably the better engineering choice in isolation — the feed is one-directional and EventSource needs no client dependency — but it would need hand-rolled per-run subscriber bookkeeping, and SignalR is the thing interviews ask about.

nodes.label: Redis backplane and sticky sessions
nodes.rationale: Required once there is more than one replica, because SignalR groups are per-process and WebSocket connections are long-lived so the load balancer must pin a client to one instance.

nodes.label: ADR-0010 Three performance tools, three different jobs
nodes.norm_label: adr-0010 three performance tools, three different jobs

nodes.label: BenchmarkDotNet (micro, in-process)
nodes.rationale: Handles JIT warmup, tiered compilation, outlier detection, statistical significance, memory diagnostics and dead-code elimination — all of which hand-rolled Stopwatch code gets wrong below about a millisecond. Pointing it at an HTTP endpoint is a category error: no concurrency, no pooling, no contention.

nodes.label: In-repo load harness (tests/Bank.LoadTests)
nodes.rationale: A dependency-free replacement for NBomber: computes RPS and percentiles from a latency array and stops there. Accepted as worse than k6 or NBomber — no ramp-up profiles, no distributed generation, no polished reporting — and risks measuring itself, mitigated by keeping it simple and async and cross-checking against the k6 scripts.

nodes.label: k6 scripts (loadtests/k6)
nodes.rationale: Would have been the better macro tool, but its binary cannot be downloaded through this environment's proxy. Scripts are committed anyway because k6 is what most teams use and they run on a developer's own machine.

nodes.label: NBomber (rejected on licence)
nodes.rationale: The original plan, dropped after reading the licence: version 3.0 (effective September 2025) is a commercial subscription whose NuGet package sets requireLicenseAcceptance and ships a licence file instead of an SPDX expression — the same disqualifier applied to MediatR and FluentAssertions in ADR-0002.

nodes.label: Benchmarking vs load testing separation
nodes.rationale: Bank.Benchmarks never makes an HTTP call; Bank.LoadTests never calls a method directly. The separation is structural so the category error is hard to make by accident. Benchmarking finds slow code; load testing finds slow systems, and the bottleneck is usually a pool or a lock that no in-process benchmark can see — evidenced by sync-over-async, which benchmarks fine and starves the thread pool under load.

nodes.label: ADR-0011 Angular standalone components + signals, no NgRx
nodes.norm_label: adr-0011 angular standalone components + signals, no ngrx

nodes.label: Standalone components with signals
nodes.rationale: The UI's whole state is the last run's result and an in-flight flag. Signals replace BehaviorSubjects without manual async pipes or subscription lifecycle. Accepted costs: no time-travel debugging, state does not survive navigation, and the approach would not scale to a large app. Routes lazy-load each page so the initial bundle stays around 85 kB gzipped.

nodes.label: NgRx (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Its benefits — shared state across distant components, time-travel debugging, disciplined mutation in a large team — do not apply to pages that share no state. The ceremony would work against the repo's purpose: a reader trying to understand a race condition should not first have to understand a reducer. A store is a coordination tool; adding one before you have a coordination problem is the same mistake as reaching for a lock you don't need.

nodes.label: ContentionHubService (degrades silently)
nodes.rationale: If the websocket never opens the page still works, because the run response carries the whole timeline. A demo that dies because a socket didn't connect is a bad demo.

nodes.label: UI holds no business logic
nodes.rationale: Every verdict — who won, who lost silently, whether money was conserved — is computed server-side by RunSummaryCalculator, because that logic is the subject being taught and it has tests. The UI cannot disagree with the tests because it computes nothing they cover. Animations are plain CSS, so @angular/animations is not a dependency and prefers-reduced-motion is one media query.

nodes.label: ADR-0012 PostgreSQL advisory locks for distributed locking
nodes.norm_label: adr-0012 postgresql advisory locks for distributed locking

nodes.label: pg_advisory_lock as distributed lock
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion on an arbitrary 64-bit key in a database already running, so no new infrastructure. Session-scoped rather than transaction-scoped because the caller may not be in a transaction; releasing is therefore ours, but disposing the context closes the connection and Postgres releases every advisory lock it held, so the lock cannot leak. Measured cost: ~2.6 s total waiting for 5 contending actors versus ~8 ms on the in-process semaphore. Only earns its place when the thing serialised is not a single database row.

nodes.label: IAccountLock abstraction
nodes.rationale: Two implementations differing only in DI registration, so one line is the entire difference between code that scales and code that doesn't. WorksAcrossInstances is exposed on the interface and surfaced through /api/lab/strategies so the UI can label which strategies survive scale-out.

nodes.label: PostgresAdvisoryAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Opens a dedicated DbContext because a session-scoped advisory lock is tied to its connection — enough concurrent holders exhausts the pool, the same failure mode as long pessimistic transactions. The Guid key is hashed into 64 bits, so two accounts can collide and share a lock: unnecessary blocking, never incorrectness.

nodes.label: InProcessAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Correct on one instance and silently wrong on three — the cliffhanger lesson 02 ends on.

nodes.label: Redis / Redlock (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Faster and the obvious production choice where Redis already runs, but adding infrastructure to teach one concept makes a lesson people skip; and a single-node Redis lock is not safe under failover while Redlock's safety is actively disputed (Kleppmann), so teaching it as settled would be wrong.

nodes.label: Fencing token
nodes.rationale: The mitigation for a TTL-based lock expiring while the holder still believes it holds it (a long GC pause is enough): a monotonically increasing number the downstream resource checks. Not needed with a Postgres advisory lock, where the connection dropping releases the lock automatically — no TTL to tune, no orphan.

nodes.label: ADR-0013 Contention events in a bounded in-memory buffer
nodes.norm_label: adr-0013 contention events in a bounded in-memory buffer

nodes.label: Bounded per-run event buffer (20,000 events, 50 runs)
nodes.rationale: Recording happens inside the code under observation, so the observer must not perturb what it observes, and it must never grow without bound — an unbounded buffer under load is just a slow memory leak. Accepted: events lost on restart, older runs 404, memory bounded but not small, and the buffer is process-local like SignalR groups.
nodes.norm_label: bounded per-run event buffer (20,000 events, 50 runs)

nodes.label: Channel<ContentionEvent> producer/consumer split
nodes.rationale: Deliberately unbounded so TryWrite always succeeds and the producer can never block; bounding it would mean either blocking a withdrawal or dropping events, and for a lab 'never distort the measurement' beats 'never allocate'. Channel<T> is async-native where BlockingCollection blocks a thread-pool thread and an event handler runs on the caller's thread.

nodes.label: Record() hot path
nodes.rationale: An Interlocked.Increment, a queue enqueue and a non-blocking channel write — no locks, no I/O, no allocation beyond the event itself. Interlocked rather than lock because a counter needs atomicity, not mutual exclusion: cheaper, and it cannot deadlock.

nodes.label: LabRunStore / RunSummary retention
nodes.rationale: RunSummary is computed once at the end of a run and stored separately, so a verdict outlives the event eviction it was derived from.

nodes.label: Persisting events to PostgreSQL or a log sink (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Persisting puts a database round-trip inside the critical section of a benchmark about database contention — the recording contends with the thing recorded. Log sinks buffer and batch on their own schedule, so ordering and latency become the framework's business, unacceptable when the ordering is the data.
nodes.norm_label: persisting events to postgresql or a log sink (rejected)

nodes.label: ADR-0014 Docker Compose replicas; Kubernetes deliberately excluded
nodes.norm_label: adr-0014 docker compose replicas; kubernetes deliberately excluded

nodes.label: Three-replica Compose demo behind nginx
nodes.rationale: The lesson is that process-local state does not survive multiple instances, and Compose shows it in about 30 seconds with a file anyone can read end to end. Accepted: Compose is not production (no rolling deploys, health routing, autoscaling or self-healing), and the demo has never been executed here — no Docker daemon, so the files are only `docker compose config`-validated.

nodes.label: Kubernetes (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Adds enormous operational surface and not one concurrency insight — manifests, a local cluster, an ingress controller and an image registry before the same demonstration. It would also mislead by implying scaling is a Kubernetes topic. Kubernetes is warranted for operational properties (rolling deploys, self-healing, autoscaling, service discovery), never to make code fast.

nodes.label: nginx round-robin (not sticky)
nodes.rationale: Breaks SignalR across replicas; documented rather than fixed with sticky sessions, because finding it yourself is more instructive than having it silently handled.

nodes.label: INSTANCE_ID per service
nodes.rationale: Injected per service and returned by /api/health and the scale endpoints, so you can see which replica served each request.

nodes.label: loadtests/k6/hot-account.js
nodes.rationale: The script that exposes the in-process lock, because it drives concurrent requests through nginx — the lab's own runner drives all actors from within one instance and therefore cannot show the failure.

nodes.label: ADR-0015 Local PostgreSQL + Respawn, not Testcontainers
nodes.norm_label: adr-0015 local postgresql + respawn, not testcontainers

nodes.label: Local PostgreSQL + Respawn test database
nodes.rationale: Chosen only because there is no /var/run/docker.sock in this build environment — the docker CLI and dockerd exist but there is no daemon to talk to. Accepted costs: an external prerequisite (dotnet test fails with a connection error, mitigated by BANKLAB_TEST_DB), possible state leaks between runs, version drift, and limited parallelism against one shared database.

nodes.label: Testcontainers (rejected on environment)
nodes.rationale: Hermetic, version-pinned and the better default where Docker exists — this ADR says it should be revisited there. It simply cannot run here: the suite would fail at fixture start.

nodes.label: PostgresFixture
nodes.rationale: Owns the connection string (overridable via BANKLAB_TEST_DB) and applies migrations once per run in InitializeAsync; shared through an xUnit collection so migrations run once rather than per test class.

nodes.label: Three isolation levers for shared-database tests
nodes.rationale: Unique data per test (what this repo does), a transaction rolled back per test, or a full Respawn reset. The middle one is the trap: it is the standard trick and silently does not work for code that manages its own transactions — exactly the pessimistic slice.
nodes.norm_label: three isolation levers for shared-database tests

nodes.label: ADR-0016 Three-tier test strategy for concurrent code
nodes.norm_label: adr-0016 three-tier test strategy for concurrent code

nodes.label: Tier 1 — deterministic forced-interleaving tests
nodes.rationale: May assert a specific interleaving and its exact consequence, because timing is fully controlled. Risk: such tests rot into documentation — a test asserting a bug happens fails confusingly if someone fixes the naive handler, unless the name and comment make the intent obvious.

nodes.label: Tier 2 — invariant / chaos tests
nodes.rationale: Free-running, so it may assert only properties that hold under every interleaving: money conserved, balance never negative, no approved withdrawal silently erased. Coverage is probabilistic — 32 actors a handful of times explores a vanishing fraction of interleavings; it raises confidence, it does not prove absence of bugs.

nodes.label: Tier 3 — integration tests against real PostgreSQL
nodes.rationale: Concurrency tokens and row locks are database behaviour; mocking them means testing the mock. Costs an external prerequisite.
nodes.norm_label: tier 3 — integration tests against real postgresql

nodes.label: Never assert an ordering you did not force
nodes.rationale: Winners.Count.ShouldBe(1) is legitimate — 100 funds exactly one 100 withdrawal under any interleaving. winners[0].ActorId.ShouldBe("actor-3") is asserting the scheduler's mood and will fail eventually. This is the rule that keeps tier 2 honest.
nodes.norm_label: never assert an ordering you did not force

nodes.label: Timing assertions must be relative, never absolute
nodes.rationale: Derived from a real M5 flake: two performance-ratio tests passed consistently, then failed under CPU saturation. The fix was deletion, not a wider threshold — a wall-clock ratio on contended shared hardware is a property of the machine, not the code, and performance claims belong to BenchmarkDotNet. whenAll < sequential / 2 survives a uniformly slower machine; whenAll < 400ms does not. Absolute lower bounds derived from the work itself are fine.
nodes.norm_label: timing assertions must be relative, never absolute

nodes.label: TimingSensitiveCollection
nodes.rationale: xUnit runs collections in parallel by default, so a test measuring 'is this faster?' was competing with three other tests for the same four cores — measuring the test runner rather than the code. The collection disables parallelisation for classes whose assertions involve elapsed time.

nodes.label: Vacuous test failure mode
nodes.rationale: An assertion so weak it can never fail — 'no exception was thrown' — while the code silently corrupts data. The naive withdrawal passes that test perfectly while destroying 400. A concurrency suite that has never gone red against known-broken code is unproven.

nodes.label: Shared invariants inherited via IWithdrawStrategy
nodes.rationale: The invariants are stated once and reused across every strategy, so a new strategy inherits the whole suite by implementing the interface. TheRaceIsDeterministic_SoTheTestIsNotFlaky runs the same forced interleaving 25 times — a test about the test infrastructure, guarding the property everything else depends on.

nodes.label: Where mutable state lives
nodes.rationale: Almost every concurrency question in the repo reduces to this. Red boxes (InMemoryAccountStore, SemaphoreSlim per account) are per process; green (PostgreSQL) is shared by every instance. Scale to three instances and the red boxes are duplicated three times — three separate stores, three sets of locks, coordinating nothing.

nodes.label: Three replicas behind nginx topology
nodes.rationale: Nothing about the code changed between the one-instance and three-replica diagrams. What changed is that `lock` now guards one third of the traffic, which is the same as guarding none of it. The database slices are unaffected because their coordination point was never in process memory.

nodes.label: A contended withdrawal, four ways
nodes.rationale: Naive loses an update because the gap between read and write leaves a stale value; the in-process lock is correct only because both actors share one semaphore object in one process; optimistic has nobody wait but the loser redo work; pessimistic has nobody waste work but the loser wait, and is a throughput disaster if the transaction is long.

nodes.label: Request path through a slice
nodes.rationale: HTTP → Endpoint.cs → Handler.cs → IInterleaveGate / store or DbContext / IContentionRecorder → SignalR hub → Angular timeline. Two files per slice, no dispatcher and no pipeline in between.

nodes.label: "Breaks down when…" column
nodes.rationale: The column that matters: senior interviews are mostly about knowing the limits of your own choices, and anyone can recite what they picked.

nodes.label: Scaling by layer (code, instances, data)
nodes.rationale: Layer 1 code: async all the way down, don't lock the hot path — one .Result anywhere measured 979 → 35 RPS, p99 105 ms → 3531 ms on identical hardware. Layer 2 instances: stateless services behind a load balancer, broken by anything in process memory including SignalR groups. Layer 3 data: shard hot rows, queue writes, read replicas, idempotency — one hot row serialises regardless of replica count, and replicas triple DB load.

nodes.label: The five sentences worth memorising
nodes.rationale: 1) A race condition is the gap between read and write, not simultaneity. 2) async is for waiting, Parallel is for working, Task.Run is neither. 3) Optimistic pays in wasted work, pessimistic pays in waiting, contention decides. 4) How you aggregate matters more than whether you parallelise. 5) Kubernetes multiplies instances; it doesn't make un-scalable code scalable.

nodes.label: Idempotency key
nodes.rationale: Gains: retries stop duplicating money. Costs: a key per operation, storage, an expiry policy. Breaks down when the client doesn't send a stable key — without one, 5 retries charged 5×.

nodes.label: One atomic statement (SET balance = balance - n WHERE …)
nodes.rationale: No coordination needed at all, but only works if the logic fits in one statement — it breaks down when your decision needs data the statement cannot see.
nodes.norm_label: one atomic statement (set balance = balance - n where ...)

nodes.label: Throttled fan-out vs unbounded Task.WhenAll
nodes.rationale: Task.WhenAll: 2005 ms → 204 ms on 5 threads, but unbounded fan-out means with 10,000 items you are your dependency's outage. Throttling with SemaphoreSlim protects the dependency and is slower on purpose (603 ms vs 204 ms); it breaks down when Release() isn't in a finally and the pool shrinks to nothing.

nodes.label: ValueTask on hot sync paths
nodes.rationale: Zero allocation versus 720 KB, but it can only be awaited once — await it twice or store it and it is worse than Task.

nodes.label: Parallel + thread-local sums (964.6 μs, 0.28× sequential)
nodes.rationale: Measured on 100,000 accounts: 3.68× faster than the 3,447.0 μs sequential baseline, versus 38,212.4 μs (11.09×) for a lock per item, 9,375.4 μs (2.72×) for Interlocked per item and 35,704.9 μs for ConcurrentQueue. Aggregation strategy dominates the decision to parallelise.

nodes.label: Task.Run wrapping sync work — 1,857× slower
nodes.rationale: 11,121.993 μs against a 6.000 μs synchronous call, allocating 1,360,216 B. async Task always-completed costs 21.43× and 720,072 B; async ValueTask costs 2.16× and allocates nothing.

nodes.label: Uncontended cost of each synchronisation primitive
nodes.rationale: Against a 352.8 μs unsynchronised baseline: Interlocked.Increment 13.66×, lock 54.61×, ReaderWriterLockSlim (write) 59.23×, SemaphoreSlim.Wait 117.31×. Ordering the primitives by cost is the point, not the absolute numbers.
nodes.norm_label: uncontended cost of each synchronisation primitive

nodes.label: ShortRun / shared-VM measurement caveat
nodes.rationale: Produced on a 4-core shared cloud VM under a ShortRun job, so some Error values are the same order as the Mean. Fine for order-of-magnitude claims (11×, 1,857×), not fine for anything subtler — two results within 2× should be treated as about the same. Stated explicitly because a benchmark you can't state the conditions for is a number, not evidence.

nodes.label: Concurrency vs parallelism (one teller vs many tellers)
nodes.rationale: Concurrency is about structure — one teller, many customers in progress, which is async/await needing no extra cores. Parallelism is about execution — four tellers at four counters, which is Parallel.ForEach and PLINQ and needs cores, because a core is a teller. Either can exist without the other.
nodes.norm_label: concurrency vs parallelism (one teller vs many tellers)

nodes.label: async is for waiting; Parallel is for working
nodes.rationale: For I/O the CPU has nothing to do while it waits, so parallelising just means more idle threads. For CPU work the CPU is the bottleneck, so async overlaps nothing. The single most common misunderstanding in .NET interviews.
nodes.norm_label: async is for waiting; parallel is for working

nodes.label: Task.Run is not async
nodes.rationale: It moves synchronous, blocking work onto a thread-pool thread and then waits for it — on a web server usually worse than doing nothing, because two threads are consumed instead of one. async all the way down means the library genuinely releases the thread.

nodes.label: Race condition = read → think → write with an intervening write
nodes.rationale: Defining it as 'two things happening at the same time' is wrong and sends you looking for the wrong fix. Nothing has to be simultaneous — on a single core one thread need only be interrupted between the read and the write. The bug is the gap, not the check, which is why more cores, async, or a ConcurrentDictionary never fix it.
nodes.norm_label: race condition = read → think → write with an intervening write

nodes.label: The three fixes: block, detect, or remove the gap
nodes.rationale: Stop anyone else writing during the gap (pessimistic locking), detect that someone did and start over (optimistic versioning), or remove the gap by making read-decide-write one atomic operation.
nodes.norm_label: the three fixes: block, detect, or remove the gap

nodes.label: Optimistic (apologise later) vs pessimistic (ask permission first)
nodes.rationale: Optimistic assumes collisions are rare and pays in wasted work, failing badly under high contention; pessimistic assumes they are common and pays in waiting, failing badly when transactions are long. Neither is better — the deciding variable is how often two people actually collide, and the trap is that both look fine in testing where you are the only user.
nodes.norm_label: optimistic (apologise later) vs pessimistic (ask permission first)

nodes.label: Concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours
nodes.rationale: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe and does not save you: TryGetValue, decide, TryUpdate is still a race. A comment saying exactly this lives in InMemoryAccountStore.
nodes.norm_label: concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours

nodes.label: Lesson 01 — Race conditions: who wins, and who loses silently
nodes.norm_label: lesson 01 — race conditions: who wins, and who loses silently

nodes.label: The lost update (measured: -400 discrepancy)
nodes.rationale: Five actors withdrawing 100 each from a 100 balance are all approved; the balance reads 0 while 500 left the bank. Every line of the naive read-think-write is defensible — no null check missing, no off-by-one — which is why reviewers approve it.

nodes.label: Silent losers
nodes.rationale: Unlike an ordinary bug, the symptom is a success response: nothing throws, nothing logs, every customer gets 200 OK. Found by an auditor months later rather than by tests. Detection in production needs invariants — a reconciliation job asserting the sum of transactions equals the balance delta; if you can't state your invariant you can't detect its violation.

nodes.label: The sawVer column — every actor read version 1
nodes.rationale: The whole bug in one column of the recorded timeline: three actors each computed 100 - 40 = 60 from the same stale snapshot and each wrote 60. The final version descends from version 1, so the intervening versions and the withdrawals they represented were erased with no error anywhere.
nodes.norm_label: the sawver column — every actor read version 1

nodes.label: RunSummaryCalculator
nodes.rationale: Decides who won by replaying writes against the version each actor read, not by comparing balances (two actors can write the same value). Works unchanged for the in-memory counter and for Postgres xmin, because it only needs versions to be unique, never ordered.

nodes.label: forceRace parameter
nodes.rationale: Makes the interleaving a parameter instead of an accident: gate.ReachAsync at InterleaveCheckpoints.AfterRead is a no-op dictionary lookup in production and a barrier in a forced run, so the lost update happens 100% of the time and a test asserts it across 25 consecutive runs. A test that catches a bug one run in twenty is a flaky test, and flaky tests get muted.

nodes.label: Why tests don't catch it — the test is the only user
nodes.rationale: WithoutContention_TheNaiveVersionIsPerfectlyCorrect passes, and so does the integration test and QA, because the bug needs a second actor to arrive during the gap and in testing there is rarely a second actor.
nodes.norm_label: why tests don't catch it — the test is the only user

nodes.label: The naive handler is correct for a single writer
nodes.rationale: Simplest and fastest — no locks, no retries, no round-trips — and genuinely right where an account is only ever written by one process in one place, such as a single-consumer queue. What makes it unacceptable for money is that it fails silently, and silent corruption is worse than a crash.
nodes.norm_label: the naive handler is correct for a single writer

nodes.label: A lock protects an invariant, not a statement
nodes.rationale: Locking only the write is pointless because the stale value was already read. The critical section must span every step that assumes the balance has not changed — ask 'what am I assuming stays true?' and lock that whole span.
nodes.norm_label: a lock protects an invariant, not a statement

nodes.label: Lock granularity: global vs per-account vs per-field
nodes.rationale: Granularity is the dial between correctness and throughput. One global lock is correct but serialises the whole bank; per-field is fastest but makes deadlock very likely. Per-entity (per account, via ConcurrentDictionary<Guid, SemaphoreSlim>) is the sweet spot: only same-account requests queue.
nodes.norm_label: lock granularity: global vs per-account vs per-field

nodes.label: SemaphoreSlim rather than lock
nodes.rationale: You cannot await inside a lock block: a monitor is owned by the thread that entered it, and an await may resume on a different thread that would release a lock it never took. SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is owned by nobody so any continuation can release it. The cost is no reentrancy and no ownership — every acquire needs exactly one release, guarded here by Interlocked.Exchange because a double release raises the count and silently admits two actors.

nodes.label: Never hold a lock across I/O you don't control
nodes.rationale: Pessimistic coordination converts other people's latency into your own. If the critical section calls an external provider taking 2 seconds, every other request for that account waits 2 seconds. Do the slow call outside the lock and re-validate inside it.
nodes.norm_label: never hold a lock across i/o you don't control

nodes.label: In-process lock: correct on one instance, silently broken on three
nodes.rationale: The semaphore dictionary is a field on one object in one process. Three replicas hold three separate semaphores for the same account id, so there is no mutual exclusion at all — the lost update returns with code that looks correct. This is the hinge of the whole repo; the strategy reports scalesAcrossInstances:false. The fix is not a better lock but moving coordination to shared state (database or distributed lock) behind the same IAccountLock interface.
nodes.norm_label: in-process lock: correct on one instance, silently broken on three

nodes.label: xmin as an EF Core concurrency token
nodes.rationale: xmin is a PostgreSQL system column holding the id of the transaction that last wrote the row; Postgres bumps it on every UPDATE for free, so it is a version counter with zero schema cost and no code to maintain. Marked IsConcurrencyToken() EF appends it to the UPDATE WHERE clause; zero rows matched raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Advantage over an application-maintained Version column: raw SQL outside EF still bumps it.
nodes.norm_label: xmin as an ef core concurrency token

nodes.label: Bounded retry loop with re-read and re-decide
nodes.rationale: Three things are easy to get wrong: a fresh DbContext per attempt (reusing one keeps the stale entity tracked so the retry re-sends the same doomed UPDATE forever), re-reading AND re-deciding rather than just re-sending the write, and bounding the retries. Unbounded retry under heavy contention is a livelock — everything busy, nothing progressing. Jittered exponential backoff belongs in production.
nodes.norm_label: bounded retry loop with re-read and re-decide

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency pays in wasted work
nodes.rationale: Measured: 5 actors, 9 attempts, 4 conflicts, 0.0 ms waited. Nobody blocks anybody; the price of a collision is rework. It degrades under contention by doing N× the work for 1× the throughput rather than by corrupting data — a better failure mode, but still a failure mode, and one that only appears under load.
nodes.norm_label: optimistic concurrency pays in wasted work

nodes.label: The hot row
nodes.rationale: One account everyone hits, a global counter, a shared inventory row. Every write conflicts with every other, so optimistic concurrency retry-storms. That is the signal to switch to pessimistic locking or to redesign the row so it stops being hot.

nodes.label: SELECT *, xmin ... FOR UPDATE row lock
nodes.rationale: Three things make it correct: it is inside a transaction (a row lock lives until the transaction ends), the read is inside the lock, and the lock is held until commit so no check-to-write window exists. xmin must be named explicitly because a system column is not returned by SELECT *. SQL Server equivalent is WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK).
nodes.norm_label: select *, xmin ... for update row lock

nodes.label: Pessimistic concurrency pays in waiting
nodes.rationale: Measured on identical input: 5 attempts, 0 conflicts, 244.1 ms waited versus optimistic's 9 attempts, 4 conflicts, 0.0 ms. Conflicts are prevented rather than detected, so nothing is redone — but total wall time is the sum of the queue, not the max.

nodes.label: Connection pool exhaustion from blocked transactions
nodes.rationale: Every blocked transaction holds a connection. Enough waiters and unrelated endpoints start failing — one of the most common causes of 'the database is down' incidents that turn out not to be the database's fault. Related failure modes: long transactions and SQL Server lock escalation.
nodes.norm_label: connection pool exhaustion from blocked transactions

nodes.label: Serializable isolation is optimistic in character
nodes.rationale: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is explicit locking, mostly orthogonal to isolation level (Postgres defaults to Read Committed). Serializable would also prevent the lost update, but by aborting transactions with a serialization failure — so you need a retry loop again, and it serialises more than intended.
nodes.norm_label: serializable isolation is optimistic in character

nodes.label: Conflict rate is the deciding variable
nodes.rationale: The question is not which is better but how often two people collide on the same row. Order-of-magnitude guidance: under 1% optimistic comfortably; 1-10% optimistic with bounded retries and jittered backoff; over 10% pessimistic, or redesign so the hot row stops being hot. Naming the deciding variable is what an interviewer listens for; 'optimistic, always' loses.
nodes.norm_label: conflict rate is the deciding variable

nodes.label: The optimistic/pessimistic crossover point
nodes.rationale: At low contention optimistic wins easily — lock-free throughput, almost nothing conflicts. At high contention pessimistic wins because optimistic's retries multiply work while throughput stays flat. Where the crossover sits depends on transaction length and conflict rate, so measure rather than guess.

nodes.label: The cheapest concurrency control is needing none
nodes.rationale: If the whole operation fits in one SQL statement — UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 40 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 40 — the database does read-decide-write atomically and there is no gap to coordinate. Reach for this first; tokens and locks are for logic that does not fit.
nodes.norm_label: the cheapest concurrency control is needing none

nodes.label: Redesigning so the hot row stops being hot
nodes.rationale: Four moves that remove the contention rather than manage it: shard the counter across N rows summed on read, queue the writes and apply them serially, event-source by appending immutable events that cannot conflict, and batch many changes into one transaction.
nodes.norm_label: redesigning so the hot row stops being hot

nodes.label: Both strategies look identical in testing
nodes.rationale: With one user there are no conflicts, so optimistic never retries and pessimistic never waits. The difference appears only under concurrency, which is exactly when experimenting is hardest. This is why the lab forces the race and why forceRace:false exists — to show how rarely the problem surfaces by chance, and therefore how easily it reaches production.
nodes.norm_label: both strategies look identical in testing

nodes.label: The four Coffman conditions
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait must all hold. Mutual exclusion is the point of locking and cannot go; the database supplies preemption by killing a victim; breaking the circular wait is nearly always the right fix because it costs one comparison and no throughput.

nodes.label: Ordered lock acquisition
nodes.rationale: Sort the two account ids and always lock the lower first, so every transaction reaches for the same account first and no cycle can form. The order is arbitrary — it only has to be consistent; primary key is stable and needs no coordination. Generalises to any number of locks. The catch is that it is a convention nothing enforces: one new code path locking in a different order reintroduces the bug, and deadlocks form between code paths, not within one method.

nodes.label: Postgres deadlock detection (SQLSTATE 40P01)
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL detects the cycle and kills one transaction, rolling its work back entirely — a deadlock costs a failed request, not corruption, and is safe to retry with bounded jittered backoff on 40P01 only (SQL Server 1205). In-process SemaphoreSlim cycles get no such favour: they hang forever with no detection, which is a real argument for pushing coordination into the database.

nodes.label: Livelock
nodes.rationale: A deadlock is stuck doing nothing; a livelock is busy achieving nothing — actors politely retrying forever, each backing off into the other. Optimistic concurrency's retry storm is the livelock risk, which is why lesson 03's retries are bounded.

nodes.label: Starvation
nodes.rationale: A third failure mode: one actor keeps losing while others progress. Common with optimistic retries under load, where the unlucky actor is always last. Fairness — a queue — fixes it; retries do not.

nodes.label: Make the timing a parameter, not an accident
nodes.rationale: With holdBetweenLocksMs at 0 the two transactions often do not overlap and no deadlock occurs — which is exactly what makes deadlocks hard to catch in testing. Widening the window makes the failure reliable, the same trick as the interleaving gate in lesson 01, and the test asserts the fix across five consecutive runs because a fix for an intermittent bug has to be proven repeatedly.
nodes.norm_label: make the timing a parameter, not an accident

nodes.label: Per-item synchronisation makes parallel slower than sequential
nodes.rationale: 400,000 items means 400,000 lock acquisitions through a single door every core must pass. Measured 164.25 ms against 18.36 ms sequential (0.11x), and 11.09x the sequential baseline in BenchmarkDotNet. ConcurrentQueue is worse still at 0.13x with 2 MB allocated — a concurrent collection is thread-safe, not fast, and is not an aggregation strategy.
nodes.norm_label: per-item synchronisation makes parallel slower than sequential

nodes.label: Partition the work, aggregate at the end
nodes.rationale: Parallel.For with localInit/localFinally accumulates privately per worker and merges about four times instead of 400,000, giving 3.68x on 4 cores — near-linear. PLINQ does the same declaratively at 2.84x and should be preferred for readability without a measured reason otherwise. How you aggregate matters more than whether you parallelise: the spread between fastest and slowest strategy is 33x with all six using every core.
nodes.norm_label: partition the work, aggregate at the end

nodes.label: False sharing
nodes.rationale: Interlocked per item (0.52x) is better than a lock — one atomic instruction rather than a synchronisation primitive — but still slower than sequential because all cores hammer one memory location and each write invalidates that cache line in the other cores' caches. Symptom: correct, parallel, and slower than expected.

nodes.label: Amdahl's law
nodes.rationale: If 10% of a job is inherently sequential then even infinite cores cap the speedup at 10x. Combined with memory bandwidth and cache limits, this is why 3.68x on 4 cores is a good result rather than a disappointment.

nodes.label: Preconditions for parallelism paying off
nodes.rationale: All four are required: genuinely CPU-bound work, enough items to cover partitioning and scheduling, expensive enough per item, and independent items. On a busy web server the server is already using every core serving requests, so parallelising one request steals from another — set MaxDegreeOfParallelism or move the work to a batch job.

nodes.label: Parallel.ForEach with an async lambda is async void
nodes.rationale: Parallel.ForEach takes Action<T>, so an async lambda becomes fire-and-forget with unobservable exceptions and returns before the work finishes. Use Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6+).
nodes.norm_label: parallel.foreach with an async lambda is async void

nodes.label: await inside a loop serialises independent calls
nodes.rationale: Each iteration waits for the previous one, so ten independent 200 ms calls take 2005 ms for no reason. The code is genuinely asynchronous — it releases the thread — it is just needlessly serialised. Async and concurrent are not the same thing, and this is one of the most common .NET performance bugs because it looks completely correct.
nodes.norm_label: await inside a loop serialises independent calls

nodes.label: Task.WhenAll fan-out
nodes.rationale: Select(...) starts each task; WhenAll launches nothing, it waits for things already in flight. Total time becomes the slowest call rather than the sum — 2005 ms to 204 ms. Beware .Select(async …) over a lazy IEnumerable enumerated twice; .ToArray() before awaiting to fix when the tasks started.

nodes.label: await releases threads rather than creating them
nodes.rationale: await Task.Delay registers a continuation and returns the thread to the pool, so ten in-flight waits cost roughly zero threads — the five observed are just whichever pool threads resumed continuations. Thread.Sleep holds its thread. At 1,000 concurrent requests each waiting 100 ms, blocking needs ~1,000 threads at ~1 MB of stack each; async needs a handful. That difference is the entire value of async on a server.
nodes.norm_label: await releases threads rather than creating them

nodes.label: Throttled fan-out with SemaphoreSlim
nodes.rationale: Unbounded WhenAll over 10,000 items fires 10,000 simultaneous calls and moves your outage to your dependency. Cap it with a SemaphoreSlim, releasing in a finally — an exception that skipped the release permanently shrinks the pool, a slow-motion deadlock that looks like the service getting gradually slower. Measured: 10 checks at concurrency 4 is 3 batches x 200 ms = 603 ms, slower than unbounded on purpose. Parallel.ForEachAsync does the same with less code.

nodes.label: Task.Run is not how you make something async
nodes.rationale: Wrapping a blocking call hides the blocking, it does not remove it, and on a server you now occupy two threads instead of one. Measured at 1,857x slower than the direct call for trivial synchronous work, allocating 1.36 MB. Async has to go all the way down. Task.Run is legitimate only for getting genuinely CPU-bound work off the request thread — and even then a background job may be the better home.
nodes.norm_label: task.run is not how you make something async

nodes.label: ValueTask on hot synchronous-completion paths
nodes.rationale: async ValueTask always-completed measured at 13.0 µs and zero allocation against async Task's 128.3 µs and 720 KB. It earns its keep on hot paths that usually complete synchronously — a cache hit, a buffered read — but it can only be awaited once, so misusing it is worse than the allocation it saves.

nodes.label: CancellationToken propagation
nodes.rationale: Threading the token through every async method is tedious and is the difference between a client disconnect freeing resources immediately and the server working on answers nobody will read. ASP.NET Core supplies the request's token for free.

nodes.label: Scaling is three questions: code, instances, data
nodes.rationale: Interviewers rarely say which of the three they mean, and the order matters. Kubernetes multiplies instances; it cannot make un-scalable code scalable. The senior closer is refusing to touch any layer before knowing which one is actually the problem — most 'we need to scale' turns out to be one N+1 query.
nodes.norm_label: scaling is three questions: code, instances, data

nodes.label: Thread-pool starvation from sync-over-async
nodes.rationale: Measured with 100 virtual users for 10 s on a 4-core VM: async 979.0 RPS with a 105.4 ms p99 against sync-over-async 35.2 RPS with a 3530.7 ms p99 — 27.8x throughput and 33.5x lower p99 with zero infrastructure change. .Result blocks a pool thread for the whole wait and the pool grows by only one or two threads per second, so 96 of 100 requests queue for a thread rather than for the database. Matching it would take ~28 instances.

nodes.label: What stateless actually means
nodes.rationale: Not 'has no state' but 'no state that matters lives in the process'. Static dictionaries, in-memory semaphores, sessions, rate-limit counters, in-process job schedulers and SignalR groups all break at more than one instance; databases, row and advisory locks, distributed caches, queues with leader election and a SignalR Redis backplane survive. Spotting the same failure across unrelated technologies is what the interview question is really testing.

nodes.label: SignalR groups are per-process (ContentionHub)
nodes.rationale: This repo has the bug on purpose: at three replicas a client connected to instance 2 misses events published on instance 1, because SignalR groups live in process memory. Same class of failure as the in-memory lock in a different costume; the fix is a Redis backplane.

nodes.label: Idempotency keys for repeated operations
nodes.rationale: Concurrency safety does not make a repeated operation safe. Five retries applied five times leave a balance of 500 against an expected 900 — every retry individually correct and concurrency-safe, the customer still charged five times. The guarantee must come from a uniqueness constraint in the database: checking 'have I seen this key?' then inserting is the read-modify-write race wearing a different hat.

nodes.label: The costs of scaling out
nodes.rationale: Every replica multiplies database load; coordination gets slower (the distributed lock took ~2.6 s of total waiting where the in-process semaphore took ~8 ms — correctness across instances costs a round-trip per acquire); debugging needs correlation ids and aggregated logging; stateless costs infrastructure (Redis, backplane, queue with leader election). Vertical scaling is underrated: a bigger machine is often cheaper and always simpler.

nodes.label: Micro-benchmarking with BenchmarkDotNet
nodes.rationale: It handles JIT warmup, tiered compilation, outlier detection, statistical significance, allocation tracking and dead-code elimination — all of which hand-rolled Stopwatch code gets wrong below about a millisecond. Never point it at an HTTP endpoint: no concurrency, no pooling, no realistic contention, and it measures a network hop as if it were code. That is a category error worth being able to name.

nodes.label: Load testing the whole system
nodes.rationale: Benchmarking finds slow code; load testing finds slow systems. A method benchmarking at 50 ns can still produce an endpoint that collapses at 100 concurrent users, because the bottleneck was the connection pool, a lock, or thread-pool starvation — none of which exist in a single-threaded benchmark. Its cost is an environment resembling production; load testing an empty database tells you almost nothing.

nodes.label: A benchmark whose conditions you cannot state is a number, not evidence
nodes.rationale: The committed reports came from a 4-core shared cloud VM under a ShortRun job, so some Error values are the same order as the Mean. Fine for order-of-magnitude claims (11x, 1,857x), not for anything subtler — two results within 2x on this hardware are 'about the same'. Saying that is worth more in an interview than a table of impressive figures.
nodes.norm_label: a benchmark whose conditions you cannot state is a number, not evidence

nodes.label: Dependency licence screening
nodes.rationale: BenchmarkDotNet is MIT and free commercially; NBomber moved to a paid commercial subscription (licence v3.0, September 2025) so the planned dependency was replaced with a small purpose-built harness in tests/Bank.LoadTests; k6 is AGPL-3.0 and its scripts are committed. Same reasoning that removed MediatR and FluentAssertions — a public teaching repo should not carry dependencies a reader cannot use at work.

nodes.label: Profile, benchmark, load test, measure in production
nodes.rationale: Do not benchmark what you have not proven is hot. Profile first (dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters), benchmark the hot method once identified, load test the system because the bottleneck usually is not the method, then measure in production. Most real problems are found at the last two steps; the satisfying numbers are at step 2, which is exactly why people over-invest there.

nodes.label: Concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours
nodes.rationale: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe and does not help: TryGetValue, decide, TryUpdate is still a race. The same argument applies to ConcurrentQueue as an aggregation strategy in lesson 07.
nodes.norm_label: concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours

nodes.label: lock vs Interlocked vs ReaderWriterLockSlim vs SemaphoreSlim cost
nodes.rationale: Interlocked is a single atomic instruction over a single variable — cheaper and cannot deadlock; lock gives mutual exclusion over a region. Measured uncontended against a plain increment: Interlocked 13.7x, lock 54.6x, ReaderWriterLockSlim 59.2x, SemaphoreSlim 117x.
nodes.norm_label: lock vs interlocked vs readerwriterlockslim vs semaphoreslim cost

nodes.label: Testing a race by making the interleaving a parameter
nodes.rationale: Not by running it a lot and hoping: an injected gate holds every actor after its read until all have read, so the lost update reproduces 100% of the time. Invariant tests then run free and assert only what must be true under any interleaving — money conserved, balance never negative — never who won, because that is asserting the scheduler. The concession to make in an interview is that this is test code in production, mitigated by compiling it out behind a flag; Coyote explores interleavings systematically rather than sampling.
nodes.norm_label: testing a race by making the interleaving a parameter

nodes.label: k6 load scenarios
nodes.rationale: The k6 binary could not be downloaded in the environment this repo was built in, so the scripts are committed for local runs and the in-repo harness (tests/Bank.LoadTests) covers the same ground with no install.

nodes.label: k6 scenario: threadpool.js
nodes.rationale: Drives async against sync-over-async to reproduce thread-pool starvation over HTTP. Target overridable with -e BASE_URL.

nodes.label: k6 scenario: hot-account.js
nodes.rationale: Contention rather than CPU is the wall — one hot account versus load spread across many. Run against deploy/docker-compose.scale.yml it is what makes the in-process lock visibly fail, because requests through nginx land on different replicas holding different semaphores.
